body:
Simon Commission: appointment and purpose

The Simon Commission, formally the Indian Statutory Commission, was appointed by the British government in November 1927. Its purpose was to examine the working of the constitutional system established under the Government of India Act, 1919, and recommend further reforms.

The commission was chaired by Sir John Simon and consisted of 7 British members. It had no Indian member. This exclusion became the central reason for nationalist opposition: Indians were being denied representation in a body appointed to decide the future of their own government.

The boycott of 1928

When the commission arrived in India in 1928, the Indian National Congress and many other political organisations organised protests. Demonstrators raised the slogan Simon Go Back.

At Lahore, nationalist leader Lala Lajpat Rai was injured during a police lathi-charge against a demonstration opposing the commission. He died on 17 November 1928, several weeks after the incident.

The commission's report

The Simon Commission published its report in 1930. Among its important recommendations were the abolition of provincial dyarchy and the expansion of provincial autonomy. However, the commission did not propose the immediate establishment of fully responsible government at the centre.

Although its report influenced later constitutional discussions, it did not itself change the law. Subsequent reforms required decisions by the British government and legislation.

Nehru Report, 1928: an Indian proposal

While Indian leaders opposed the exclusion of Indians from the Simon Commission, representatives of different political groups also attempted to formulate their own constitutional proposals. An All Parties Conference appointed a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru. Its report, submitted in 1928, became known as the Nehru Report.

The committee that prepared the Nehru Report was chaired by Motilal Nehru, not Jawaharlal Nehru. The two leaders must not be confused in questions concerning the report.

Principal recommendations

  • Dominion status: India should enjoy a constitutional position comparable to other self-governing dominions within the British Commonwealth, with its own responsible parliamentary government.
  • Responsible government: The executive should be accountable to the legislature rather than remain primarily under uncontrolled colonial authority.
  • Fundamental rights: The proposed constitution should protect civil liberties, including freedom of religion and legal safeguards for personal liberty.
  • Adult franchise: The proposed elected House of Representatives and provincial councils were to be based on voting rights for eligible men and women aged 21 years or above.
  • Joint electorates: Members of different communities should generally vote in common electorates, rather than through separate electorates organised exclusively by religion.
  • Minority representation: The report provided for population-based seat reservations for Muslim minorities and for non-Muslims in the North-West Frontier Province, but no communal seat reservations in Punjab or Bengal.

Joint electorates and separate electorates

Under a joint electorate, eligible voters belonging to different religious communities participate in a common electoral process. Under a separate electorate, voters from a particular community elect representatives through an electorate restricted to that community.

The Nehru Report favoured joint electorates but did not reject every form of minority seat reservation. This distinction is important: reservation of seats and separate electorates are not identical arrangements.

Political response and the demand for independence

The Nehru Report did not secure agreement among all major political groups. Disagreements concerned the constitutional position of Muslims, minority safeguards and the distribution of powers. In 1929, Muhammad Ali Jinnah set out his 14 Points, which included demands for stronger minority protections.

Meanwhile, the Congress moved beyond dominion status. At its Lahore session in December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, it adopted the goal of Purna Swaraj, or complete independence.

The essential comparison

The Simon Commission was a British-appointed investigating body whose members were all British. The Nehru Report was an Indian constitutional proposal prepared under Motilal Nehru. The former reviewed existing arrangements; the latter proposed what India's future government should look like.

Prelims focus

  • Simon Commission appointed: 1927; arrival in India: 1928.
  • Chairman: Sir John Simon; membership: 7 British members and no Indians.
  • Lala Lajpat Rai died on 17 November 1928.
  • Nehru Report: 1928; chairman: Motilal Nehru.
  • Nehru Report supported dominion status, fundamental rights and joint electorates.
  • Trap: The Nehru Report sought dominion status; the Congress adopted complete independence as its goal in December 1929.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed p. 120; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 2, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 62–63; Nehru Report, 1928, recommendations NR.1, NR.4, NR.10, NR.33 and NR.86–NR.89, Constitution of India historical documents archive, consulted 22 November 2026; UK House of Lords Library, Lord Sinha of Raipur and the Government of India Act 1919, 2019, pp. 3–4.]

pictures.alt: The British Simon Commission prompted protests; the Indian Nehru Report proposed dominion status, followed by Congress adopting Purna Swaraj in 1929.
pictures.caption: The Simon Commission and the Nehru Report represented different approaches to constitutional change.

title: Simon Commission and Nehru Report: British Review versus Indian Constitutional Proposal

body:
Purpose of the conferences

The Round Table Conferences were 3 meetings held in London between 1930 and 1932. They brought together representatives invited by the British government to discuss India's future constitution.

The discussions followed years of demands for responsible government, opposition to the Simon Commission and disagreement about the political representation of different communities. Major questions concerned the relationship between British India and the princely states, the powers of central and provincial governments, and safeguards for minorities.

First Round Table Conference, 1930–1931

The First Round Table Conference was held from November 1930 to January 1931. Representatives of the princely states, British political parties and various Indian communities attended.

The Indian National Congress did not participate. At the time, the Congress was conducting the Civil Disobedience Movement and was unwilling to accept negotiations under the existing conditions.

Because the Congress was a leading organisation in the nationalist movement, its absence limited the conference's ability to secure broad political agreement.

Gandhi–Irwin Pact and the Gujarat connection

The Civil Disobedience Movement had begun in 1930 with Gandhi's Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram, near Ahmedabad, to Dandi on the Gujarat coast. The protest challenged the British salt law and became an important expression of mass resistance.

On 5 March 1931, Mahatma Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin concluded the Gandhi–Irwin Pact. Gandhi agreed to suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement, and the Congress agreed to participate in the next Round Table Conference. The government agreed to measures including the release of political prisoners not convicted of violence.

The pact directly connects a major movement originating in Gujarat with constitutional negotiations in London.

Second Round Table Conference, 1931

The Second Round Table Conference was held from September to December 1931. Mahatma Gandhi attended as the sole official representative of the Indian National Congress.

The discussions considered federal arrangements and minority representation, but serious disagreements remained. The conference failed to produce an accepted constitutional settlement. Gandhi returned to India without securing the agreement sought by the Congress.

Third Round Table Conference, 1932

The Third Round Table Conference took place during November–December 1932. The Congress again did not participate.

Further discussions informed the British government's later constitutional proposals. The broader sequence of conferences, reports and parliamentary deliberations contributed to the framework enacted through the Government of India Act, 1935.

Why the conferences did not settle the dispute

A new constitution required agreement not merely on how many Indians would hold office, but also on how power would be divided between the centre, provinces and princely states. Political organisations and community representatives disagreed over the extent of self-government and the safeguards needed for their interests.

The conferences were therefore significant constitutional negotiations, not sessions of the Indian National Congress and not legislative bodies that independently enacted the 1935 Act.

Prelims focus

  • Total Round Table Conferences: 3.
  • Venue: London; period: 1930–1932.
  • First Conference: 1930–1931; Congress absent.
  • Gandhi–Irwin Pact: 5 March 1931.
  • Second Conference: 1931; Gandhi was the sole official Congress representative.
  • Trap: Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference, not the First or Third.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 2, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 63–65; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Chapter 13, Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, discussion of the Salt March and Round Table Conference; UK Parliament, 1931 Indian Round Table Conference, Living Heritage collection, consulted 22 November 2026; Government of India, Round Table Conference, Second Session, proceedings, 7 September–1 December 1931.]

pictures.alt: British and Indian delegates in period clothing discuss constitutional arrangements around long tables in a formal London chamber in 1931.
pictures.caption: Delegates assembled in London to discuss India's future constitutional arrangements in 1931.

pictures.alt: Congress was absent from the First and Third Round Table Conferences; Mahatma Gandhi attended the Second as its sole official representative.
pictures.caption: Congress participation differed across the 3 Round Table Conferences.

title: Round Table Conferences, 1930–1932: Negotiating India's Constitutional Future

body:
Why the Cripps Mission came to India

During the Second World War, Britain wanted Indian political cooperation in the war effort. Indian nationalists, however, opposed a situation in which India was involved in the war without possessing an independent national government.

In March 1942, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India with proposals for a future constitutional settlement. Cripps was a senior British political leader, and his visit became known as the Cripps Mission.

The principal proposals

Dominion status after the war

Britain proposed that a new Indian Union would be established after the war, with dominion status. This would give India substantial powers of self-government within the Commonwealth framework. It was not an offer to establish an immediately independent government during the war.

A constitution-making body

The proposals envisaged a body to frame India's future constitution after the war, with British Indian representatives elected by proportional representation by the provincial lower houses acting as 1 electoral college, and princely-state representatives appointed by their rulers.

Possibility of provincial non-accession

An important provision allowed a province unwilling to accept the new constitution to remain outside the proposed Indian Union and retain its existing constitutional position, subject to arrangements for its future status.

This provision created concern about the possibility of constitutional fragmentation. It did not, by itself, establish Pakistan or formally divide British India into 2 independent states.

British control of defence during the war

Defence would remain under British responsibility during the war. This was a critical limitation because Indian leaders wanted an effective transfer of power, not merely a promise of constitutional change after the conflict ended.

Why the proposals were rejected

The Indian National Congress rejected the proposals because they did not provide an immediate transfer of effective political authority, particularly over defence. Congress leaders also objected to the provision under which provinces could remain outside a future Indian Union.

The All-India Muslim League was also dissatisfied. The proposals did not explicitly accept its demand for a separate sovereign Pakistan.

With no accepted settlement, the mission failed. The wider political confrontation continued, and the Congress launched the Quit India Movement later in 1942.

Cripps Mission and Cabinet Mission: the basic distinction

The Cripps Mission was a 1942 wartime offer that emphasised a constitution to be made after the war and allowed provincial non-accession. The Cabinet Mission, which arrived in 1946, tried to establish an immediate constitution-making process and proposed a united Indian arrangement with limited central powers.

Sir Stafford Cripps was associated with both missions: he led the 1942 mission and was 1 of the 3 members of the Cabinet Mission in 1946.

Prelims focus

  • Cripps Mission: March 1942.
  • Leader: Sir Stafford Cripps.
  • Proposed dominion status: after the Second World War.
  • Proposed constitution-making body: to be formed under post-war arrangements.
  • Provinces could decline to join the proposed Indian Union.
  • Trap: The mission did not offer immediate Indian control over wartime defence.

[British Government, Cripps Constitutional Proposals, March 1942, reproduced in Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Volume 10, section Cripps Proposals, Dr. Ambedkar Foundation, Government of India, consulted 22 November 2026; Jawaharlal Nehru correspondence concerning the Cripps Mission, March 1942, historical archival records.]

pictures.alt: Cripps Mission, March 1942: British wartime defence responsibility, promised post-war dominion status and constitution-making, provincial opt-out, and rejection.
pictures.caption: The Cripps proposals distinguished immediate wartime arrangements from a promised post-war settlement.

title: Cripps Mission, 1942: Wartime Offer and the Demand for Immediate Self-Government

body:
The Indian National Army and the war

The Indian National Army (INA), also known as the Azad Hind Fauj, was an armed force formed during the Second World War with the aim of ending British rule in India. It included Indians who had been prisoners of war in Southeast Asia, along with other volunteers.

The INA initially developed under Mohan Singh. It was later reorganised and led by Subhas Chandra Bose, who became closely associated with its campaign for Indian independence. The INA operated with Japanese assistance against British forces.

After Japan's defeat in 1945, many INA personnel came into British custody. The British authorities decided to prosecute selected officers for offences arising from their participation in the INA.

The first major Red Fort trial

The best-known INA trial began on 5 November 1945 at the Red Fort in Delhi. It was a court-martial, meaning a trial conducted by a military court.

The 3 officers tried together were:

  • Shah Nawaz Khan.
  • Prem Kumar Sahgal.
  • Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon.

The central charge concerned waging war against the British Crown. The authorities regarded service in the INA against British forces as a punishable military offence. The defence argued that the officers had acted in pursuit of Indian independence.

Defence lawyers and public response

Bhulabhai Desai played a leading role in defending the INA officers. Other prominent figures associated with the defence included Jawaharlal Nehru and Asaf Ali.

The prosecution generated widespread sympathy for the accused. Many Indians viewed the officers as patriots who had fought against colonial rule. The 3 defendants belonged to different religious communities, and their joint trial became a powerful symbol of nationalist solidarity.

Public demonstrations and support for the INA prisoners increased pressure on the colonial government. The reaction also raised concern among British military authorities about the political feelings of Indian soldiers.

Verdict and remission of sentences

The military court found the officers guilty and imposed punishments that included transportation for life, dismissal from military service and loss of pay and allowances.

On 3 January 1946, the punishment of transportation for life was remitted by the Commander-in-Chief, Claude Auchinleck. Remission means that an imposed punishment is cancelled or reduced by an authority empowered to do so. The officers were consequently released from custody.

Importance for the independence movement

The trials helped spread knowledge of the INA's activities among the Indian public and generated a strong sense of solidarity across political and community lines. They became one of the important developments in the final phase of the struggle against British rule.

However, the INA trials should not be confused with the INA's formation or its military campaigns. The trials occurred after the Second World War, when captured personnel were prosecuted by British authorities.

Prelims focus

  • INA: Indian National Army; also called Azad Hind Fauj.
  • Leader strongly associated with the INA: Subhas Chandra Bose.
  • First major Red Fort trial began: 5 November 1945.
  • Accused officers: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon.
  • Leading defence lawyer: Bhulabhai Desai.
  • Trap: The trial was held at the Red Fort in Delhi, and the punishment of transportation for life was remitted on 3 January 1946.

[M. C. Setalvad, Bhulabhai Desai, Publications Division, Government of India, chapter INA: Red Fort Trial, printed pp. 307–339, 2010 reprint; Colonel S. K. Bose, Impact of INA on India's Struggle for Independence, United Service Institution of India Journal, July–September 2011, opening section, p. 1, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The Red Fort trial opened on 5 November 1945, sparked nationalist mobilisation, and was followed by remission and release on 3 January 1946.
pictures.caption: The Red Fort court-martial became a national political issue rather than remaining only a military prosecution.

title: Indian National Army Trials, 1945–1946: Red Fort and Nationalist Mobilisation
